tn.quote: Fròʔò has three level tones, high (H), mid (M) and low (L). There are no contour tones. The syllable is the tone bearing unit (TBU) and every syllable in every word carries its own tone, regardless of the category and the length of the word. In other words, all vowels in the language bear one of these three tones. ... Tones play a large role in the grammatical domain, as exemplified in (1), where a change in grammatical tone signifies a change in tense/aspect/mood of the utterance. ... Combinations of tones in the nominal domain reveal the existence of floating tones in part of the vocabulary

3073.dloc: Ch. I §B.1.c p. 30 ('unités accentuelles'); §B.2 'L'accent des mots isolés' p. 32; §B.3 'L'accent des groupes enclitiques' p. 34
3073.heavy: Long syllables, i.e. syllables with a long (or surlong) vowel or closed syllables: 'Les syllabes longues, et par conséquent les voyelles longues, attirent sans doute dans certaines limites l'accent principal' (p.31 h); 'Toute syllabe fermée est nécessairement longue, que son centre soit une voyelle brève ou longue' (Avis important p.13; cf. p.126 G.1.b(2) 'Toute syllabe fermée est longue'); rule d(1) 'Les noms de plus de 3 syllabes, l'antépénultième étant de quantité longue' is exemplified by closed short-vowel antepenults (tilắẓẓiwîn 'fards', iġə́nnawän 'cieux') beside long-vowel ones (tinâriwîn 'plaines', inâlmâdän 'élèves') (p.33); intensive verbs accent 'la première, le cas échéant l'unique, voyelle allongée' (p.34 g.1); surlong vowels are 'presque toujours munies de l'accent principal' (p.26 e). Light = open syllable with a short vowel ('Les voyelles centrales ə et ä sont de quantité brève', Ch. I opening page p.17; breve-marked ă ĭ ŭ ĕ ŏ, Avis §1 p.14). Special case: in trisyllabic sg. nouns a penult 'brève ou fermée par une gém.' (nouns ending in a vowel, a.1) or 'fermée par une géminée' (a.2, 'Cette règle demande des vérifications ultérieures') sends the accent to the antepenult with rythme creux (p.32), whereas a penult closed by a consonant cluster keeps it (ănắbdun, c.1; 'l'influence des noms à groupe consonantique au lieu de la géminée', a.2).
3073.dflt: penult: 'Tous les noms sg. ou pl. de 3 syllabes ou moins, exceptés ceux du § a' and 'Tous les verbes de 3 syllabes ou moins sans voyelle longue' (pp. 32-33 c.1-2)
3073.prule: Non-contrastive word accent, mainly pitch-realised, placed inside a right-edge window according to quantitative syllable structure and word class: default penult for all nouns of <=3 syllables and all verbs of <=3 syllables without a long vowel; antepenult (with 'rythme creux') for trisyllabic vowel-final sg. nouns whose penult is short (ə ä ă ĭ ŭ ĕ ŏ) or geminate-closed, for plural classes 2/3/4/7 and trisyllabic pronouns; antepenult ('rythme égal') for nouns of >3 syllables with a long antepenult; intensive verb forms accent their first long vowel wherever it falls; final accent for masc. numerals 1-10, pf. int. with long final vowel, and a few words like kălá 'non'. Long syllables/vowels 'attract the principal accent within certain limits'.
3073.srule: Prasse distinguishes three accent degrees, one on every syllable: principal (high tone, slight dynamic increase), secondary (mid tone), tertiary (low tone). Placement of the non-principal degrees is 'a matter of rhythm': in the normal 'rythme égal' the pitch rises stepwise to the principal accent and falls stepwise after it, so the syllables adjacent to the principal carry secondary accent and those further out tertiary (3-2-1-2-3); in the 'rythme creux', required by the antepenult/pre-antepenult classes of §B.2.a-b (e.g. áġənnà 'ciel': acute = principal on the antepenult, unmarked penult = tertiary, grave = secondary on the final; p.136 §G.2.a(1) defines ´ principal, ` secondary, tertiary = unaccented), a tertiary syllable stands next to the principal and the secondary lies beyond it (2-3-1-3-2). In enclitic groups a word that does not carry the group's principal accent keeps a secondary accent on the syllable that would be accented in isolation (§B.1.f(1)). These are graded pitch levels around a single principal accent, not rhythmic (alternating) stresses.

3073.sec_quote: La distinction des accents secondaire et tertiaire est un problème de rythme. Le rythme musical normal est une montée progressive vers l'accent principal et une descente progressive après lui. Autrement dit les syllabes à accents principal et tertiaire se trouvent séparées par celles à accent secondaire (3-2-1-2-3). [...] certains mots [...] demandent un rythme différent [...] (2-3-1-3-2)

secx.sec_quote_tr: The distinction between secondary and tertiary accent is a matter of rhythm. The normal musical rhythm is a progressive rise towards the principal accent and a progressive descent after it. In other words the syllables with principal and tertiary accent are separated by those with secondary accent (3-2-1-2-3). [...] certain words [...] require a different rhythm [...] (2-3-1-3-2)

tn.quote: C’est e[ss]entiellement un accent musical avec des variations dynamiques peu prononcées. ... a) Chaque syllabe peut être prononcée avec l’un des trois accents suivants: (1) L’accent principal, qui comporte un ton haut et une légère augmentation de l’effort dynamique. (2) L'accent secondaire qui comporte un ton moyen et un effort dynamique moyen. (3) L'accent tertiaire qui comporte un ton bas et un effort dynamique moyen. ... L'accent n’a donc pas de fonction phonologique. Il n’existe pas de paires de mots qui se distinguent uniquement par (la place de) l’accent.
tn.translation: It is essentially a musical accent with little-pronounced dynamic variations. ... a) Each syllable can be pronounced with one of the following three accents: (1) the principal accent, which involves a high tone and a slight increase in dynamic effort; (2) the secondary accent, which involves a mid tone and a medium dynamic effort; (3) the tertiary accent, which involves a low tone and a medium dynamic effort. ... The accent therefore has no phonological function. There are no pairs of words distinguished solely by (the place of) the accent.
tn.cite: Prasse, Karl-G. 1972. Manuel de grammaire touarègue (tăhăggart), I-III: Phonétique - Écriture - Pronom. Copenhague: Éditions de l'Université de Copenhague. Ch. I, sect. B 'L'accent', pp. 30-34.
tn.locator: p. 30-31, Ch. I sect. B.1 'Generalites' a-c
tn.note: Non-contrastive musical word accent: one high-pitched principal accent per word/enclitic group, place set by syllable quantity and word class; 3 degrees = rhythm, not tonemes.

3074.heavy: Stress-attracting ('heavy') = a syllable whose peak is any vowel other than /ɨ/; stress-repelling ('light') = a syllable whose peak is /ɨ/ (high central unrounded vowel; phonemic per OPD p.2, e.g. pɨne 'fat', nɨ 'mother'; functionally the system's colourless/reduction vowel: Grammar Essentials p.6 says /ɨ/ 'When preceded by /w/ or /y/ it is pronounced as [ʊ] or [ɪ] respectively' and /a/ 'approaches that of /ɨ/ when unstressed in word final position'). Source wording: 'unless that syllable peak is /ɨ /... until it reaches a vowel other than /ɨ/'.
3074.dflt: Not stated as a rule. The OPD does not say where stress falls if the penult and every syllable to its left have /ɨ/ peaks, nor whether a final full vowel could then attract stress. Grammar Essentials p.6 (scan p.11) data, verified on my 600-dpi crop: disyllables whose only non-final vowel is the /ɨ/ penult carry stress on that penult (wɨkae [wˈʊgæ] 'sweat', yɨme [jˈɪmɪ] 'grub'; the /ɨ/ is glide-coloured to [ʊ]/[ɪ] there). When the penult is a full vowel the default is simply the penult (grid 10 010 0010 00010 000010 0000010 00000010).
3074.prule: Default penultimate stress; if the penult's peak is the high central vowel /ɨ/, stress retracts leftward, without stated bound, to the nearest syllable whose peak is a vowel other than /ɨ/.

3075.dq: primary stress normally fell on the next to last syllable, but on the final syllable of a multisyllabic word which ended in [e], [i], or one of the nasalized vowels, as in Manatí, burén ('griddle'), Maniabón.

3075.prule: Stress non-phonemic. Primary stress normally on the penultimate syllable, but on the final syllable of a polysyllabic word ending in [e], [i], or a nasalized vowel (Manatí, burén 'griddle', Maniabón); a final orthographic <x> (possibly = [h]) also seems to mark final stress fairly frequently. The rule is a philological inference from Las Casas's and Oviedo's acute-accent usage relative to 16th-century Spanish accentuation rules; the authors call the statements 'admittedly problematic'.
3075.quote: Las Casas is usually very careful to indicate which syllable bears strong stress, and Oviedo frequently does so as well. Generally speaking, the chroniclers wrote Taíno words and used the acute accent (') to stress syllables which did not abide by the Spanish rules of accentuation - last syllable if the word ended in a consonant other than n or s, the next to last syllable if the word ended in a vowel, with exceptions indicated by the acute accent mark. 3084.tone: Tanacross is a high-marked lexical tone language: every syllable is lexically specified low or high, stem syllables also rising, falling and extra-high (Holton 2000 sec. 2.3, pp.72-86; tone summary p.86). Stress is mentioned only in passing (sec. 5.1 terminology; sec. 6.6 particles); there is no stress section, and the acoustic chapter (ch. 3) measures pitch and phonation, not stress. Holton 2005 pp.264-266: intonational central tones align with the (final) stem syllable, but in one HLL imperative / wh-question pair the middle syllable is called 'most prominent' because spread high tone precedes a low stem tone -- a pitch effect of tone, not a stress exception.

3085.prule: No Tandroy-specific rule sentence is in any reachable source. The first-hand stress-marked Tandroy data (Adelaar 2019, c.100 stress-marked TDR tokens) show penultimate stress on every polysyllable except words ending in a weak (whispered-vowel) final syllable -kĕ/-tsĕ/-ŋĕ/-ñĕ, which carry antepenultimate stress (trùkĕ, tùmbukĕ, làtakĕ, hàtukĕ, aŋàraŋĕ, tahìnaŋĕ, hùŋgutsĕ, tùmitsĕ, nùfutsĕ, fisafùaŋĕ, fiheŋàraŋĕ) with the single exception fivavèŋĕ 'vagina (polite)' (penult + weak final -ŋĕ, Table 4 p.81); no Tandroy form is final-stressed. The source's own characterisation of the system is 'Malagasy stress is contrastive' (p.60), and the group-level rule it matches (Howe 2017 p.48, scoped over the Southwestern dialects incl. Tandroy) is 'Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable' with antepenultimate stress on weak-final -ke/-tse words 'and a small number of words have final-syllable stress'. Coded lexical (contrastive stress with a strong penultimate default), matching the catalog's coding of Central Malagasy plat1254.

3087.dloc: Ch. VI 'L'accent tonique', pp. 236-237; Ch. III p. 164 for the Antanosi proparoxytons; cf. p. 201, p. 153, pp. 237-238 for suffix/compound rules, Introduction pp. XXXIX and XLVII (pp. 43, 51) for dialect identity.
3087.prule: No single placement rule is stated: the accent falls within the last three syllables of the root and is lexically distributed. Disyllabic roots are 'generally' paroxytone (penult), 'very rarely' oxytone (áti 'liver' vs atí 'here'); trisyllabic roots are 'generally' proparoxytone (antepenult), 'sometimes' paroxytone, 'very rarely' oxytone (tánana 'hand' vs tanána 'village' printed side by side); quadrisyllabic roots are antepenult or penult; monosyllables are accented. The antepenult class coincides with roots ending in a weak whispered final syllable (Merina -tră/-kă/-nă = Antanosi -tsĕ/-kĕ, pp. 164, 201: 'les finales... des proparoxytons sont généralement prononcées tsĕ, celles des paroxytons ts[ĕ over i]; l'une et l'autre sonnent rarement tsi'); oxytones have a short accented final vowel; the accented vowel of paroxytons/proparoxytons is long. Suffixation moves the accent one syllable to the right; compounds and reduplications keep the accent only on the last member.
3087.srule: None: one tonic accent per word. Ferrand's summary rules: the accented vowel of paroxytone/proparoxytone roots 'est longue et tonique... Toutes les autres voyelles du thème radical sont brèves' (1°); when a suffix moves the accent the former tonic becomes 'brève atone' (2°); reduplications and compounds 'ne conservent l'accent tonique que sur... le dernier élément du mot composé' (3°). No secondary or rhythmic accent is described anywhere in Ch. VI (pp. 236-245).

3090.prule: Two contrastive register tones (high marked, low unmarked; all tonal patterns contrast in 1-3-syllable words). Stress is non-contrastive and predictable from tone within the phonological word (1-5 syllables): monosyllables are stressed whatever their tone; in level-tone polysyllables (all-high or all-low) every syllable is stressed; in mixed-tone polysyllables every high-toned syllable is stressed; a high-toned syllable immediately followed by a single low-toned onsetless (V) syllable takes primary stress, and every other stressed syllable is secondary. No positional (initial/penult/final) or weight rule is given.
3090.srule: Tone-determined, not rhythmic: every stressed syllable other than the primary is secondary ('cualquier otra sílaba acentuada es secundaria'), i.e. every high-toned syllable in mixed-tone words and every syllable in level-tone words carries stress, with primary on the high-toned syllable followed by a single low-toned V syllable and secondary on all the others, e.g. /útía/ ['ú"tíà] 'abeja', /yúkúuruka/ 'tambor'.

3094.prule: No word stress: the author could detect no consistent loudness difference between the syllables of a word, and earlier impressions of 'stress' resolved on checking into falling or high pitch or phonetically long vowels. 3094.tone: Healey 1964 sec. 7-7.4: two tonemes UP and DOWN; each short syllable nucleus carries one toneme (a few contracted syllables carry two); no co-occurrence limits between tonemes within a word; long final nuclei carry one toneme, long initial nuclei two (7.4); pitch shape of the first (sometimes second) toneme of a word is allophonically conditioned by the final toneme of the preceding word (10.1c); the first vowel of a word is ultra-short and quality-neutralised (2.2, 6.2-6.3). Sec. 10.2 offers an equivalent HIGH/LOW register analysis (toneless first vowel, floating word-final toneme that attaches to the next word's first vowel or, before a final intoneme, to the word's own last syllable, giving utterance-final glides); author keeps the step analysis on elegance grounds. Sec. 7.3 states that apparent 'stress' was falling/high pitch or vowel length. 3096.prule: No word stress is described. Tembo is a mora-counting two-tone language: every mora, including a word-initial syllabic nasal, carries H or L (F and R are HL/LH combinations); nominal tone patterns are of the 'unrestricted' type (roughly 2^n patterns for an n-mora word, words up to 7 moras); the isolation form's tone is basic; downdrift but no downstep; no vowel-length contrast (VV sequences reduce to one mora, no lengthening before NC). Kaji 2001 (English summary, p. 37) sums it up: 'each mora in principle should be marked either as high, low, falling or rising... Tembo, therefore, can be characterized as a polymoraic tone language', as against accentual Haya and 'bound accent' Swahili.
3096.srule: Not mentioned in Kaji 2021 (ch. 6, pp. 109-140, read in full): the chapter describes lexical H/L tone on every mora and never mentions stress, secondary stress or rhythmic prominence for Tembo; its only use of 'accent' (fn. 7, p. 111) concerns Swahili, contrasted with Tembo's lexical H.

tn.translation: The basic tones of Tembo, as in many other African languages, are two: high level H and low level L. Phonetically, however, combinations of H and L give rise to a falling tone F as in (1a) and a rising tone R as in (1b). ... Note that in Tembo a syllable (more precisely a mora) consisting of a single word-initial nasal also carries tone. ... As a phonetic modification of tone Tembo has the phenomenon called downdrift: an H after an L is realized slightly lower. ... Downstep does not occur. ... The TRU of Tembo is the mora, not the syllable.

3098.prule: No word-stress rule. Tem is described by every modern first-hand source as a two-tone (H vs L) language; Tchagbalé 2001 re-analyses the H tone as a pitch accent ('accent tonal') tied to grammatical morphemes (the obligatory final class/infinitive suffix is 'accentué'; the accent is fixed on, or floats left/right of, its morpheme), with at most one H per word and no lexical tone contrast among words of the same category. The only mention of dynamic stress is Müller 1905's hedged impression ('scheint mir') that intensity accent stays within the final three syllables, seldom on the antepenult, and shifts under plural suffixation — no position fixed, no rule.

3098.tone: Tchagbalé 2001 abstract: 'Chaque syllabe de mot tem est dotée d'un niveau mélodique particulier qui est le haut ou le bas; ces deux niveaux pratiquent, dans la chaîne, le downdrift et le downstep. Mais, en même temps, il est impossible d'opposer un mot d'une catégorie grammaticale à un autre de la même catégorie par le ton; la syllabe ne peut accueillir plus d'un ton; la constitution du schème tonal de mot n'est pas libre; bref toutes choses contraires à la nature et à la fonction du ton.'... 'nous soutenons, aujourd'hui que derrière les tons haut et bas du Tem, il y a un accent tonal.' §3.1.1: 'De tous ces affixes susceptibles d'entourer le radical nominal, seul le dernier suffixe est obligatoire; lui seul a la forme forte et est accentué'. §4 Conclusion: 'Il ressort de notre étude que le Tem a un accent qui, en surface, se manifeste par deux tons haut et bas. Le ton haut exprimant la présence d'accent et le ton bas exprimant l'absence d'accent.... Le Tem est donc une langue à accent tonal.' Tchagbalé 1984 (JWAL 14(1): 29-30, scan verified by the compilers): 'celui que, provisoirement, nous appelons th (ton haut) en attendant de voir s'il ne s'agit pas plutôt d'un accent'... tn.quote: Il ressort de notre étude que le Tem a un accent qui, en surface, se manifeste par deux tons haut et bas. Le ton haut exprimant la présence d' accent et le ton bas exprimant l' absence d' accent. Expression de surface, les deux tons organisent un niveau autonome qui élabore des règles de comportement telles que le downdrift et le downstep, indépendamment de l' accent; des règles qui, parfois, rendent l' accent invisible … Le Tem est donc une langue à accent tonal.
tn.translation: It emerges from our study that Tem has an accent which, on the surface, is manifested by two tones, high and low: the high tone expressing the presence of accent and the low tone expressing the absence of accent. As a surface expression, the two tones organise an autonomous level that develops rules of behaviour such as downdrift and downstep, independently of the accent; rules which sometimes make the accent invisible … Tem is therefore a tonal-accent (pitch-accent) language.
tn.cite: Tchagbalé, Zakari. 2001. L'accent tonal du Tem. In Ulrike Gut & Dafydd Gibbon (eds.), Proceedings of TAPS: Typology of African Prosodic Systems Workshop, Bielefeld University, May 18-20, 2001 (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1). Web edition, 17 pp., unpaginated.
